    Working with GeoZarr¶

    GeoZarr is a set of conventions to describe geospatial raster data stored as Zarr. In this notebook we use rio-tiler's experimental AsyncGroupReader to read data from GeoZarr groups (hierarchies of groups and arrays, with optional multiscales/overviews).

    The reader is built on top of zarr-python (async API) and obstore and enables you to:

    • list the variables (arrays) available in a GeoZarr hierarchy
    • read previews, tiles, parts or features from one or more variables
    • select or reduce non-spatial dimensions (e.g. time)

    Variables are referenced using {group}:{array_name} (e.g. measurements/reflectance:b02).

    Requirements

    python -m pip install "rio-tiler[zarr]" matplotlib

    Note: the rio_tiler.experimental module is subject to change. The reader is async, so the cells use top-level await (supported in Jupyter).

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import numpy
import zarr

# zarr's `ObjectStore` adapts an obstore store so zarr-python can use it
from zarr.storage import ObjectStore

# obstore provides fast (Rust based) access to HTTP/S3/GCS/Azure storage
from obstore.store import HTTPStore
from matplotlib.pyplot import imshow

# Experimental async reader for GeoZarr groups (emits a RioTilerExperimentalWarning on import)
from rio_tiler.experimental.zarr import AsyncGroupReader

    Sentinel-2 L2A (EOPF)¶

    The first dataset is a Sentinel-2 L2A product from the EOPF Sample Service, stored as a GeoZarr with multiple resolution levels (r10m, r20m, r60m, ...).

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    # Sentinel-2 L2A product converted to GeoZarr by the EOPF project.
# Note: the root group doesn't define spatial/proj conventions, so the
# dataset level bounds/crs default to WGS84 and a global extent.
src_path = "https://titiler-benchmark-public.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/geozarrs/S2C_MSIL2A_20260810T125031_N0512_R095_T26SMJ_20260810T155917.zarr"
    # Sentinel-2 L2A product converted to GeoZarr by the EOPF project. # Note: the root group doesn't define spatial/proj conventions, so the # dataset level bounds/crs default to WGS84 and a global extent. src_path = "https://titiler-benchmark-public.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/geozarrs/S2C_MSIL2A_20260810T125031_N0512_R095_T26SMJ_20260810T155917.zarr"

    Open the GeoZarr¶

    We use an obstore HTTP store, wrapped in a zarr ObjectStore, to open the root group of the dataset.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    # Create an obstore HTTP store pointing at the root of the GeoZarr
# (for data on S3/GCS/Azure you could use `S3Store`, `GCSStore` or `AzureStore` instead)
store = HTTPStore(src_path)

# Wrap the obstore store so it can be used by zarr-python (read-only access)
zarr_store = ObjectStore(store=store, read_only=True)

# Open the root group (async API)
# Only the metadata is fetched here, no array data is read yet
geozarr = await zarr.api.asynchronous.open_group(store=zarr_store, mode="r")
    # Create an obstore HTTP store pointing at the root of the GeoZarr # (for data on S3/GCS/Azure you could use `S3Store`, `GCSStore` or `AzureStore` instead) store = HTTPStore(src_path) # Wrap the obstore store so it can be used by zarr-python (read-only access) zarr_store = ObjectStore(store=store, read_only=True) # Open the root group (async API) # Only the metadata is fetched here, no array data is read yet geozarr = await zarr.api.asynchronous.open_group(store=zarr_store, mode="r")

    Dataset information¶

    AsyncGroupReader.info() returns the dataset level metadata and the list of available variables.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    # Initiate the reader with the root group
# The reader walks the hierarchy to find the groups/arrays with spatial information
reader = AsyncGroupReader(input=geozarr)

# Get general information about the dataset (bounds, crs, variables, ...)
info = await reader.info()
print(info.model_dump_json(indent=2))
print()

# Variables are identified by `{group}:{name}`
# and this is the name you'll pass to the `variables=` option of the read methods
print("List of Available Variables")
print([var["long_name"] for var in info.variables])

    Preview¶

    preview() returns a low resolution version of the whole variable(s). For multiscale groups, the reader will select the most appropriate resolution level.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    # Read a preview of the variable "measurements/reflectance:b02" (blue band)
# The reader picks the best resolution level (multiscale) for the output size (1024px max by default)
img = await reader.preview(variables=["measurements/reflectance:b02"])

# `img` is a rio-tiler `ImageData` object
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Names:", img.band_names)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (bands, height, width)

# Reflectance values are float, rescale 0 -> 0.2 to 0 -> 255 for display
# `data_as_image()` returns the data as a (height, width, bands) array, as expected by matplotlib
imshow(img.rescale(((0, 0.2),)).data_as_image())

    # Create a True Color preview from the red (b04), green (b03) and blue (b02) variables
# Variables are stacked along a new `variables` dimension, in the requested order
# Note: all variables need to have the same spatial grid (they are in the same group here)
img = await reader.preview(
    variables=[
        "measurements/reflectance:b04",  # red
        "measurements/reflectance:b03",  # green
        "measurements/reflectance:b02",  # blue
    ]
)
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (3, height, width)

# Apply the same 0 -> 0.2 rescaling to the 3 bands
imshow(img.rescale(((0, 0.2),)).data_as_image())

    Read data for a Feature¶

    feature() reads the data intersecting a GeoJSON feature. The returned ImageData is in the dataset's CRS and masked outside the geometry.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    # Area of Interest (GeoJSON Feature, in WGS84)
# Note: coordinates are (longitude, latitude)
feat = {
    "type": "Feature",
    "properties": {},
    "geometry": {
        "type": "Polygon",
        "coordinates": [
            [
                [-28.103158369086685, 39.126003460944304],
                [-27.875051234256915, 39.126003460944304],
                [-27.875051234256915, 38.96740726058968],
                [-28.103158369086685, 38.96740726058968],
                [-28.103158369086685, 39.126003460944304],
            ]
        ],
    },
}

# Read the data within the feature as a False Color composite (NIR, Red, Green)
# Vegetation (high NIR reflectance) will appear in red
# Note: the feature is expected in WGS84 by default (use `shape_crs=` for other CRS)
img = await reader.feature(
    feat,
    variables=[
        "measurements/reflectance:b08",  # NIR
        "measurements/reflectance:b04",  # red
        "measurements/reflectance:b03",  # green
    ],
)

# Pixels outside the geometry are masked
imshow(img.rescale(((0, 0.25),)).data_as_image())
    # Area of Interest (GeoJSON Feature, in WGS84) # Note: coordinates are (longitude, latitude) feat = { "type": "Feature", "properties": {}, "geometry": { "type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [ [ [-28.103158369086685, 39.126003460944304], [-27.875051234256915, 39.126003460944304], [-27.875051234256915, 38.96740726058968], [-28.103158369086685, 38.96740726058968], [-28.103158369086685, 39.126003460944304], ] ], }, } # Read the data within the feature as a False Color composite (NIR, Red, Green) # Vegetation (high NIR reflectance) will appear in red # Note: the feature is expected in WGS84 by default (use `shape_crs=` for other CRS) img = await reader.feature( feat, variables=[ "measurements/reflectance:b08", # NIR "measurements/reflectance:b04", # red "measurements/reflectance:b03", # green ], ) # Pixels outside the geometry are masked imshow(img.rescale(((0, 0.25),)).data_as_image())

    Band math¶

    Because rio-tiler returns ImageData objects, we can use apply_expression to compute indices such as the NDVI.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    # Read the NIR (b08) and Red (b04) variables within the feature
img = await reader.feature(
    feat,
    variables=["measurements/reflectance:b08", "measurements/reflectance:b04"],
)

# Rename bands so we can use them in the expression
# (by default the bands are named after the `variables` dimension)
img.band_names = ["nir", "red"]

# Compute the NDVI
# `apply_expression` returns a new ImageData with one band per expression
img = img.apply_expression("(nir - red) / (nir + red)")

# NDVI values are in the -1 -> 1 range, rescale them to 0 -> 255 for display
imshow(img.rescale(((-1, 1),)).data_as_image())
    # Read the NIR (b08) and Red (b04) variables within the feature img = await reader.feature( feat, variables=["measurements/reflectance:b08", "measurements/reflectance:b04"], ) # Rename bands so we can use them in the expression # (by default the bands are named after the `variables` dimension) img.band_names = ["nir", "red"] # Compute the NDVI # `apply_expression` returns a new ImageData with one band per expression img = img.apply_expression("(nir - red) / (nir + red)") # NDVI values are in the -1 -> 1 range, rescale them to 0 -> 255 for display imshow(img.rescale(((-1, 1),)).data_as_image())

    Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 RTC¶

    The second dataset is a Sentinel-1 Radiometric Terrain Corrected (RTC) datacube, with ascending and descending groups containing vv/vh backscatter arrays with a time dimension.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    # Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 RTC GeoZarr
# Note:
# - the root group doesn't define spatial/proj conventions, so the dataset
#   level bounds/crs default to WGS84 and a global extent
# - variables in the ascending/descending groups (vv/vh) have a time dimension (time, y, x)
src_path = "https://titiler-benchmark-public.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/geozarrs/s1-rtc-32UPB.zarr"
    # Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 RTC GeoZarr # Note: # - the root group doesn't define spatial/proj conventions, so the dataset # level bounds/crs default to WGS84 and a global extent # - variables in the ascending/descending groups (vv/vh) have a time dimension (time, y, x) src_path = "https://titiler-benchmark-public.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/geozarrs/s1-rtc-32UPB.zarr"
    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    # Create the obstore/zarr stores and open the root group
# (same steps as for the Sentinel-2 dataset)
store = HTTPStore(src_path)
zarr_store = ObjectStore(store=store, read_only=True)
geozarr = await zarr.api.asynchronous.open_group(store=zarr_store, mode="r")
    # Create the obstore/zarr stores and open the root group # (same steps as for the Sentinel-2 dataset) store = HTTPStore(src_path) zarr_store = ObjectStore(store=store, read_only=True) geozarr = await zarr.api.asynchronous.open_group(store=zarr_store, mode="r")
    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    # Initiate the reader
reader = AsyncGroupReader(input=geozarr)

# Get general information about the dataset
info = await reader.info()
print(info.model_dump_json(indent=2))
print()

# Each variable is listed per orbit direction (e.g `ascending:vv`, `descending:vh`)
print("List of Available Variables")
print([var["long_name"] for var in info.variables])

    Working with non-spatial dimensions¶

    When a variable has extra (non-spatial) dimensions, rio-tiler will, by default, flatten them into bands. Use:

    • sel: a list of {"dimension": ..., "values": ..., "method": ...} selectors to select one (or more) value along a dimension (label based, or position based when the dimension has no coordinates). The optional method controls inexact matches (nearest, pad/ffill, backfill/bfill)
    • reduce: to reduce a dimension with a function (e.g. numpy.ma.mean)
    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    # Without selection, all the time steps are returned as bands
# Note: there are no `time` coordinates, so band names default to `time{n}`
img = await reader.preview(variables=["ascending:vv"])
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Names:", img.band_names)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (number of time steps, height, width)

# The 3 time steps are displayed as an RGB image
# (colors show the backscatter changes between the dates)
imshow(img.data_as_image(), vmin=0.05, vmax=0.4)

    # Select a specific time slice
# Note: because the `time` dimension has no coordinates, selection is done by position
# (here the first time step)
img = await reader.preview(
    variables=["ascending:vv"],
    sel=[{"dimension": "time", "values": 0}],
)
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Names:", img.band_names)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (1, height, width)

# Single band, displayed with matplotlib's default colormap
imshow(img.data_as_image(), vmin=0.05, vmax=0.4)

    Multi-variable composite¶

    Selection applies to all requested variables, which are then stacked along a new variables dimension.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    # Create a VV/VH/VV composite for the first time step
# The `sel` selector is applied to each variable before stacking them
# Note: the same variable can be requested more than once
img = await reader.preview(
    variables=["descending:vv", "descending:vh", "descending:vv"],
    sel=[{"dimension": "time", "values": 0}],
)
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Names:", img.band_names)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (3, height, width)

# Backscatter values are small floats, so we set `vmax` to stretch the display
imshow(img.data_as_image(), vmax=0.15)
    # Create a VV/VH/VV composite for the first time step # The `sel` selector is applied to each variable before stacking them # Note: the same variable can be requested more than once img = await reader.preview( variables=["descending:vv", "descending:vh", "descending:vv"], sel=[{"dimension": "time", "values": 0}], ) print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions) print("Band Names:", img.band_names) print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions) print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape) # (3, height, width) # Backscatter values are small floats, so we set `vmax` to stretch the display imshow(img.data_as_image(), vmax=0.15)

    # Create a VV;VH;VV/VH composite for the first time step
img = await reader.preview(
    variables=[
        "descending:vv",
        "descending:vh",
    ],
    sel=[{"dimension": "time", "values": 0}],
    # The bands are named `variables1` (`vv`) and `variables2` (`vh`), in request order,
    # and the `expression` uses those names. `;` separates the output bands.
    expression="variables1;variables2;variables1/variables2",
)
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Names:", img.band_names)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (3, height, width), one band per expression

# Each band has its own value range, so we use a per-band rescaling
# (`rescale` updates the ImageData in place)
img.rescale(((0, 0.3), (0, 0.05), (0, 25)))
imshow(img.data_as_image())

    Temporal reduction¶

    Instead of selecting a single time step, we can reduce the time dimension (here with a masked mean) to create a temporal composite.

    In [25]:
    Copied! 
    # Create a VV/VH/VV composite, reducing the time dimension with a (masked) mean
# `reduce` takes a list of (dimension, function) tuples
# The function is called with the `axis` of the dimension to reduce
# (any numpy reducer works, e.g. numpy.ma.median, numpy.ma.max, ...)
img = await reader.preview(
    variables=["descending:vv", "descending:vh"],
    reduce=[("time", numpy.ma.mean)],
    # The bands are named `variables1` (`vv`) and `variables2` (`vh`), in request order,
    # and the `expression` uses those names. `;` separates the output bands.
    expression="variables1;variables2;variables1/variables2",
)
print("Dimensions:", img.dimensions)
print("Band Names:", img.band_names)
print("Band Descriptions:", img.band_descriptions)
print("Array Shape:", img.array.shape)  # (3, height, width), the time dimension is gone

# Each band has its own value range, so we use a per-band rescaling
# (`rescale` updates the ImageData in place)
img.rescale(((0, 0.3), (0, 0.05), (0, 25)))
imshow(img.data_as_image())
